question: Compare list.sort() and sorted() in Python.
answer: list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None [S1]/ [S3], while sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original list unchanged [S2]/ [S3] [S1].

citations.title: Python Debugging Playbook
citations.text:
3. Lookup Errors Compared
KeyError is raised when a dictionary key is missing. IndexError is raised when a sequence index is
out of range. AttributeError is raised when an object has no attribute of that name.
The message 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' almost always means a variable holds
None instead of a list. The classic cause is writing nums = nums.sort(), because list.sort() sorts in
place and returns None. Use nums.sort() on its own line or sorted(nums) when a new list is
needed.
dict.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError, while collections.defaultdict(list) creates a missing key with
an empty list the first time it is accessed, which makes grouping code shorter.

citations.title: Python Lecture Notes
citations.text: 4. Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries A list is an ordered, mutable sequence: nums = [3, 1, 2]. Common methods are append(x) to add at the end, insert(i, x), remove(x), pop() to remove and return the last item, and sort() to sort in place. The built-in sorted(nums) returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged. List comprehensions build lists concisely: [n * n for n in nums if n > 1]. A tuple is an ordered but immutable sequence, written (1, 2). Tuples are used for fixed records and can be dictionary keys because they are hashable. A set stores unique, unordered elements and supports fast membership tests plus union (|), intersection (&) and difference (-). A dictionary maps keys to values: ages = {"Ali": 20, "Mona": 22}. citations.title: Python Reference Notes
citations.text:
BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS
len(x) returns the number of items in x.
sum(nums) adds the numbers in an iterable.
min(nums) and max(nums) return the smallest and largest items.
sorted(items) returns a new sorted list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
enumerate(items) gives (index, item) pairs.
zip(a, b) pairs items from two iterables and stops at the shortest.
range(stop) generates 0 .. stop-1; range(start, stop, step) supports steps.
isinstance(x, int) tests whether x is an instance of a type.
